abstract: Rapid evolution in one species can restructure ecological communities, but how its effects vary across environmental conditions remains poorly understood. Here we mapped the consequences of antibiotic resistance evolution in Aeromonas caviae across 64 combinations of resource availability and antibiotic stress in three- and 16-species bacterial communities. Resistance evolution changed where community-state boundaries were located, with boundaries lost or gained depending on resource availability. The same evolutionary change increased diversity in some environments but decreased it in others. Species success was partly explained by growth traits at zero or low antibiotic concentrations and by intrinsic resistance at inhibitory concentrations. Resistance evolution reversed dominance between the two dominant species and changed which traits mattered. It also altered other species' responses below inhibitory concentrations, mostly between closely related species. Our findings show that the consequences of evolution depend on environmental context but can be partly explained by species traits.
